items.title: AI溢价：估值中真的有AI吗？
items.snippet: [依据PitchBook 2026年Q2估值数据，分析巨额交易中的AI成分是否真正支撑高估值，探讨AI溢价是否名副其实。]
items.raw_snippet:
According to PitchBook’s Q2 2026 valuations data, megadeals of $100m or more took 87.5% of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of the year, with AI companies alone capturing 86% of total U.S. venture funding. The median increase in an AI company’s valuation from one round to the next was 2.2x, against 1.6x for non-AI companies. This increased to a median 6.6x increase at series D funding round and beyond. [...] Put “AI-powered” on a pitch deck and a $10m company starts to look like a $100m one. Add “agentic” and “AI-native,” and someone in the room will ask whether $500m is too conservative.

  The enthusiasm isn’t irrational. AI can restructure costs, automate knowledge work, and accelerate scientific discovery. But the size of an opportunity and a company’s present value are different numbers, and that gap is where a fund earns or loses its returns. [...] The market isn’t simply funding AI. It’s paying for its possibility, which is wonderful, especially when someone else is footing the bill.

  ## Adoption is not differentiation

  An investment committee’s first question should be simple: What economic value exists because of AI that wouldn’t exist without it?

  Not whether the company uses AI. Nearly every company does; that’s like asking whether it has email.

# Jay Ramnundlall: Why Human Accountability Must Remain At The Centre Of AI Governance

No photo availableCIO Africa authorBySteve Mbego  

10 min read

As AI assumes greater control over business decisions, Jay Ramnundlall, CEO, Alpvest Institute of FutureTech, calls for stronger human oversight, board accountability and leadership. [...] We can delegate intelligence, but the responsibility for what has been delegated must remain in human hands.

Where should accountability for AI decisions ultimately rest: with the CIO, CEO, board or organisation?

Ramnundlall: The board is ultimately accountable for governance. Before approving autonomous AI systems, it has a responsibility to define their parameters at the design stage. [...] Jay Ramnundlall, CEO, Alpvest Institute of FutureTech (AIFT)

Artificial intelligence is moving beyond generating reports, answering questions and recommending decisions. Increasingly, organisations are deploying AI agents capable of executing instructions, approving transactions and interacting directly with corporate systems.

For business leaders, this transition presents a difficult question: when an AI system acts independently and something goes wrong, who takes responsibility?
